subtitle: The words of the news, and reported speech with the Konjunktiv I
words.intro: At eight every evening, a very serious person on German television tells the nation what somebody else said. German has a special verb form for this, so that the newsreader can never be blamed.

grammar[0].fact: German has a strict division: federal government (*Bund*), sixteen states (*Länder*), towns (*Gemeinden*). Schools and police belong to the states, so a family moving from Bavaria to Berlin may find their child ahead or behind.

grammar[1].fact: In everyday speech, Germans mostly use the indicative or *würde* for this. The Konjunktiv I is the voice of news, courts and science. A friend who says *Er sagte, er sei krank* sounds as if they don’t quite believe it, which may be intended.

document.caption: Ein Plakat in Bochum: Was wird gefordert?
document.intro: A real poster from a local vote in Bochum in 2008. Parents wanted to save a grammar school from closing. It is short and loud, the opposite of the news. Your job is to make it calm: report what it says.
document.fact: A local vote like this one is binding, if enough people turn out. It is decided by a simple yes or no, and the poster shows the X where it should go. *Statt* takes the genitive in good German, but a poster leaves that out.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Report it with the Konjunktiv I.
reading.intro: A local TV station has one news story tonight: a goat has been seen on the town hall roof. The press spokesman, Herr Dr. Lenz, gave a statement. Vroni is reading it out on air, with all the distance the Konjunktiv I can provide.
reading.fact: The *Tagesschau* at 8 p.m. has been on since 1952. It is still read from a desk, and millions watch. Its *Konjunktiv I* is a kind of legal insurance: *Der Minister sagte, er sei unschuldig* reports the claim without saying it is true.
reading.tasks[1].instruction: Complete with the Konjunktiv I from the text.
